item.title: An Improved Graph Attention Network for Semantic Segmentation of Industrial Point Clouds in Automotive Battery Sealing Nail Defect Detection
item.description:
The problem

Sealing nails plug the electrolyte injection holes of automotive batteries and are laser-welded in place. Welding can leave defects such as bursts, molten beads and pinholes that compromise the battery’s safety and durability. The metal surface is highly reflective and textureless, which makes 2D imaging unreliable: it needs frequent lighting re-tuning and suffers from high false-detection rates. Traditional inspection therefore combines 2D vision to locate a defect with 3D vision to measure it, a multi-stage workflow that is complex, less efficient and accumulates errors from one stage to the next.

A 3D point cloud gives direct access to the shape of the surface, but many state-of-the-art segmentation networks, such as Point Transformer and Swin3D, rely heavily on RGB-D or intensity input. That limits their robustness when only geometry is available, which is common on reflective industrial parts. The defects themselves are also hard to learn. Defects of the same type can take very different shapes, a scan of about 100,000 points contains only about 1,000 defect points, and near a defect boundary the point coordinates barely differ from those of the surrounding surface.

How it works

LGASS (Local Graph Attention for Semantic Segmentation) segments defects directly in the 3D point cloud, so localisation and measurement happen in a single stage. It uses geometry only: the network input is each point’s surface normal, and the point coordinates determine which points are neighbours. The network is a U-Net-style encoder–decoder built around two new modules, one for attention and one for pooling.

  1. Scan the weld. A 3D laser profiler (OPT-LPC20, blue 405 nm laser stripe) scans the sealing nail at a lateral resolution of about 0.05 mm. An improved RANSAC algorithm fits the reference planes of the nail and the battery cover, and a circular region around the nail’s centre isolates the weld region for inspection.
  2. Watch the normals. Nearly every defect region shows clear changes in height and surface normal. Near a defect boundary, two adjacent points can have almost the same coordinates but clearly different normals, so the difference in normals between neighbours is a key indicator of a defect.
  3. Local Graph Attention Filter (LGAF). Each point is linked to its k nearest neighbours. LGAF computes attention weights from the correlation between a point’s own feature and its feature differences to each neighbour, weighted by their spatial distance, and aggregates the neighbours’ features with these weights. A large normal difference produces a high attention weight, which focuses the network on defect boundaries.
  4. Spatial Attention Graph Pooling (SAG-Pooling). When the encoder downsamples, each point is scored by multiplying a learned spatial attention weight with its normal difference to a neighbour. Only the top-ranked points are kept, so points survive only if they are both spatially important and geometrically distinctive, such as those on defect edges.
  5. Label every point. The decoder uses graph-convolution blocks with positional encoding to upsample back to the full point set, with skip connections from the encoder. It assigns each point one of six classes: normal surface or one of the five defect types (burst, pit, warpage, molten bead, pinhole). A class-weighted loss gives the rarer defect classes more influence during training.

Results

mIoU 79.26% and overall accuracy 99.43% on the sealing-nail dataset (mean of five runs), ahead of PTv3 (75.13% mIoU) and OA-CNN (74.04%) (Table 4).
Pinhole IoU 65.23%, against at most 60.04% for the compared methods (Table 4).
+2.59 points mIoU from LGAF and SAG-Pooling together over a baseline with standard graph convolution and pooling (Table 5).
220.9 ms to process one sample on an RTX 4070 GPU (Table 6).

The authors built a new dataset for this work from real sealing nails on inspection lines, with naturally occurring defects: 271 normal and 658 defective samples covering five defect types (170 burst, 112 pit, 132 warpage, 102 molten bead and 142 pinhole; Table 1). Code and dataset are released online. LGASS was compared with GACNet, PointNet, PointNet++, Point Transformer (PTv1 and PTv3) and OA-CNN in this geometry-only setting. Over five runs with different random seeds its mIoU stayed between 78.97% and 79.61%, and it achieved the best IoU on four of the five defect classes: pit, molten bead, warpage and pinhole.

The ablations show where the gain comes from. Replacing graph convolution with LGAF adds 2.19 points of mIoU, SAG-Pooling alone adds 0.46, and the two together add 2.59 (Table 5). Normals are the better input: with normals only the network reaches 79.23% mIoU, against 76.94% with coordinates only and 78.31% with both (Table 7). The class-weighted loss raises IoU on the minority classes, by 2.3 points for pinholes and 2.13 for molten beads, and lifts mIoU from 78.73% to 79.26% (Table 8). Inference needs about 2.8 GB of GPU memory. The authors note that LGASS may struggle with highly concave geometry, such as recessed nails with overlapping defects, where a fixed k-nearest-neighbour graph limits long-range context, and that rare classes such as pinholes still have lower IoU than the others.

item.title: Dynamic correlation network and structure-aware matching for robust point cloud registration
item.description:
Relative rotations between point clouds pose significant challenges for reliable correspondence estimation. This work proposes a rotation-robust registration framework that integrates a Dynamic Correlation Network (DCN) with Structure-Aware Point Matching (SAPM), using rotation-equivariant features, adaptive feature correlation, and bidirectional correspondence consistency to stabilize matching under unseen orientations.

This work appears in Computers & Graphics, 104672.

Algorithm principle

This paper targets rotation-robust point cloud registration. A major weakness of many learned registration methods is that rotation augmentation cannot densely cover the continuous SO(3) space, so feature correlations become unstable when test-time rotations differ from training-time rotations.

The proposed framework combines a Dynamic Correlation Network (DCN) with Structure-Aware Point Matching (SAPM). DCN starts from rotation-equivariant features and dynamically assembles local feature correlations with adaptive channel and spatial weighting, then reasons in a rotation-invariant feature space. SAPM refines patch-level and point-level correspondences with contextual interactions and bidirectional consistency, so the final matching stage is less dependent on brittle single-point similarities or RANSAC-style cleanup.

Visual evidence

Overall DC-SAM architecture. Rotation-equivariant feature extraction is followed by dynamic correlation modeling and structure-aware correspondence refinement.

Point-level correspondences after structure-aware matching. The module uses neighborhood context and bidirectional consistency to suppress unstable matches.

Indoor registration examples on 3DMatch/3DLoMatch-style scenes, where rotation variation and partial overlap make correspondence selection difficult.

Outdoor KITTI registration examples showing that the same matching strategy transfers from indoor RGB-D scans to LiDAR-scale scenes.

Results and impact

Experiments on indoor benchmarks (3DMatch and 3DLoMatch) and outdoor KITTI data show stronger accuracy and robustness under varying rotations than recent registration baselines. The main practical contribution is not only higher registration quality, but a registration pipeline that remains stable when the relative orientation is outside the narrow distribution seen during training.

item.title: SuP: Sub-cloud Driven Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two 3D scans of the same scene. Modern methods do this precisely when the two scans share a lot of geometry. In applications such as large-scale mapping and autonomous navigation, though, the views often share only a small part of the scene. Once the shared surface falls below about 30 %, classic ICP and learned methods alike struggle to find reliable correspondences, and registration slows, drifts or fails.

The paper traces these failures to the regions that are not shared: they can still be geometrically or semantically similar to each other, and matching the two whole clouds then produces wrong correspondences that obscure the correct ones. Earlier work tried to predict which points lie in the overlap, but that prediction depends on consistent features and becomes less effective on low-overlap pairs. Later methods strengthen the features with attention, geometric encodings, semantics or colour, yet their accuracy still drops as overlap falls.

How it works

SuP changes what it looks for. Two scans may overlap only a little overall, but if each is cut into smaller pieces and the pieces are matched pairwise, a subset of these sub-cloud pairs has high overlap. SuP calls these high-overlap pairs anchor pairs. It finds them in two phases, then builds its matches only from inside them.

  1. Features for the whole scan. A KPConv backbone extracts point features at several scales, and attention layers exchange context within and between the two scans. By default SuP uses the colour-enhanced backbone and attention of ColorPCR.
  2. Subdivide. Each scan is split into k sub-clouds. Farthest point sampling picks well-spread centroids, and each sub-cloud collects a centroid’s nearest neighbours within a radius.
  3. Phase I: overlap-guided prior weighting (OPS). For every source–target pair of sub-clouds, SuP measures how strongly their point features agree, counting only mutual top matches, and keeps the best-scoring pairs as candidates. This is an efficient first filter against pairs that do not overlap.
  4. Phase II: multi-scale post-weighting (MPN). Each candidate pair is aligned with a preliminary pose from a weighted SVD. A small learned network then checks whether points that now sit close together also have similar features, at two scales. The pairs with the highest feature-consensus weights become anchor pairs. During training, the network is supervised by how well each candidate actually aligns (an alignment-aware weighting loss).
  5. Merge-to-match. Inlier correspondences from all anchor pairs are merged, refined on the denser points, and passed to a standard estimator (RANSAC or the RANSAC-free LGR) to compute the final rotation and translation.

In the reported setup, each scan is cut into 6 sub-clouds, giving 36 possible pairs. OPS keeps 24 of them, and the top 8 by feature consensus become anchor pairs.

Results

Registration recall 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch with the RANSAC-free LGR estimator, the highest among the methods compared with LGR (Table 2).
98.1 % and 90.4 % with RANSAC, and the highest registration recall at every sampling level from 5,000 down to 250 correspondences (Table 1).
Lowest pose errors: 1.374° / 0.046 m on Color3DMatch and 2.493° / 0.074 m on Color3DLoMatch (Table 3).

The evaluation uses colour-enhanced versions of the indoor 3DMatch benchmark: Color3DMatch, with pairs overlapping by more than 30 %, and Color3DLoMatch, the harder split with 10–30 % overlap. Registration recall is the share of scan pairs aligned to within 0.2 m RMSE. SuP uses ColorPCR’s colour-enhanced backbone by default; compared with ColorPCR alone, the strongest baseline, it raises recall from 96.5 % to 97.8 % on Color3DMatch and from 88.3 % to 90.2 % on Color3DLoMatch under LGR. The share of correct matches rises as well: with 250 sampled correspondences on Color3DLoMatch, 76.0 % of SuP’s matches are correct (inlier ratio), against 68.0 % for ColorPCR.

The sub-cloud step also works as an add-on to other methods. Added to GeoTransformer, it raises Color3DLoMatch recall from 74.0 % to 76.7 %; added to PEAL, from 81.2 % to 83.4 % (Table 4). In the ablation study, adding the four components one at a time (OPS, the feature-consensus weights, MPN and the alignment-aware loss) raises recall at every step on both benchmarks (Table 5). Sub-cloud size matters as well: smaller sub-clouds may lower recall because of insufficient overlap, larger ones miss local detail, and the default radius setting τ = 0.35 gives the best balance (Table 6). The paper’s limitation section notes that features from scans captured with very different sensors could weaken OPS and MPN, and suggests feature normalisation or domain adaptation as a next step.

item.title: SemReg: Semantics-Constrained Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
The problem

Point cloud registration finds the rotation and translation that line up two partially overlapping 3D scans of the same scene, so that they can be merged into one. Recent learned methods describe every point by the shape around it, let the two scans exchange information through cross-attention, and then match points. Shape alone is often ambiguous, though: partial scans of a bed and a table can look geometrically alike. Cross-attention also lets every region of one scan interact with every region of the other, including pairs that are unlikely to overlap, such as a chair in one scan and a table in the other. These superfluous interactions lead to wrong matches.

Indoor scans captured with RGB-D cameras come with colour images, and semantic understanding is far more mature for 2D images than for 3D geometry. An earlier cross-modal method, PCR-CG, added image colour to the 3D features, but it uses only colour, not the semantic content of the images, and its features remain inconsistent.

How it works

SemReg is a 2D–3D cross-modal network. It keeps a standard 3D backbone for shape features and adds a semantic signal taken from the RGB frames, which it uses in three places: inside attention, at matching time, and in the training loss.

  1. Two scans with their colour frames. The input is a pair of partially overlapping point clouds, each with its RGB images. A KPConv backbone downsamples each cloud and extracts local shape features.
  2. Semantic features from the images. A pretrained DINOv2 network, kept frozen, extracts features from the RGB images. Using depth and the camera parameters, these are projected onto the 3D points and added to the shape features in self-attention.
  3. A semantic prior guides cross-attention. For each source point, SemReg finds the target points whose semantic features closely resemble its own and places a Gaussian over 3D distance around each one. The mixture of these Gaussians, the Gaussian Mixture Semantic Prior (GMSP), weights cross-attention so that features interact mainly between semantically similar regions.
  4. Matching within similar semantics. The Semantics Constrained Matching module sets the score of a candidate pair to zero when the semantic prior says the two points belong to unrelated regions. During training, a Semantics Aware Focal Loss supervises only pairs that are semantically related.
  5. Pose from the surviving matches. The final rotation and translation are estimated from the correspondences with RANSAC, and can be refined further with ICP.

Results

Registration recall 94.7 % on 3DMatch and 75.9 % on 3DLoMatch, the highest of all methods compared on both (Table 1).
95.4 % and 77.4 % after ICP refinement (Table 2).
Replacing all four semantic components with standard counterparts drops recall to 92.1 % and 66.5 % (Table 3).

The evaluation uses 3DMatch, an indoor RGB-D benchmark, and its low-overlap split 3DLoMatch (scan pairs with 10–30 % overlap). Registration recall is the share of scan pairs whose estimated transformation is accurate to within 0.2 m (RMSE). SemReg leads on both splits, ahead of SIRA-PCR on 3DMatch and GeoTransformer on 3DLoMatch, and in the paper’s ICP-refinement comparison its margin over the next-best method grows to 1.5 and 2.9 points. The semantic components matter most when overlap is small: they account for 9.4 points of recall on 3DLoMatch, against 2.6 points on 3DMatch. In one extreme case with 12.53 % overlap, where the only shared object is a chair, the semantic prior still locates the chair in the target scan and the registration succeeds, while GeoTransformer fails.

SemReg matches at a coarse level, with 0.1K–1K correspondences per pair against 6K–7K for dense methods such as GeoTransformer. Its inlier ratio is therefore lower than that of some competitors, although its registration recall is higher. Results on the outdoor KITTI dataset are reported in the supplementary material. The method needs RGB images aligned with the scan, so it does not apply directly to standalone point clouds; the authors suggest rendering images from the point cloud as a future workaround.

item.title: TopFormer: Topology-Aware Transformer for Point Cloud Registration
item.description:
Point cloud registration requires finding reliable correspondences between two scans of the same scene. Transformer-based methods have improved on classical descriptor matching by using attention to capture global context, yet they remain vulnerable to scenes with repetitive geometric motifs—tiled floors, uniform walls, symmetric objects—where many local regions appear nearly identical. TopFormer tackles this robustness gap by enriching transformer feature tokens with topological structure descriptors that capture how each surface point connects to its neighbours at multiple scales. These topological features provide information not available in standard geometric or learned local descriptors: two patches that look locally similar may have different global connectivity signatures, making them distinguishable. TopFormer integrates these topology-aware tokens into a standard transformer matching pipeline with minimal added complexity. Presented at the International Conference on Computational Visual Media (CVM) 2024, the method achieves competitive or superior registration recall on 3DMatch and KITTI benchmarks, with the clearest gains on the challenging low-overlap evaluation split where conventional attention-based methods degrade most.

Problem setting

Transformer-based point cloud registration methods have achieved strong performance by matching local geometric descriptors with global attention, but they still struggle in scenes with repetitive geometry or limited texture where local shape alone is insufficient to distinguish correspondences. TopFormer addresses this by incorporating topological structure descriptors—derived from persistent homology or graph connectivity of the local neighbourhood—into the transformer feature tokens. These topology-aware tokens encode how each point sits within the broader surface topology, providing a complementary discriminative signal that reduces false matches in symmetric or repetitive regions.

item.title: A Point Cloud Contour Extraction Method based on Plane Segmentation
item.description:
This work extracts contour features from object point clouds through a two-stage pipeline. A PCA-guided RANSAC step segments the dominant planes; the segmented planar points are then projected to 2D, where gradient analysis recovers the surface contours. The method is aimed at industrial inspection, where the contours of interest are often incomplete or weakly defined.

This work appears in Frontiers in Computing and Intelligent Systems, 7(2):21-25.

Problem setting

A two-stage pipeline extracts contour features from object point clouds. First, the Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC) plane fit is guided by Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to segment the dominant planar regions. The segmented planar points are then projected to 2D, and contour features are extracted from the projection using gradients.

item.title: Gap measurement method based on projection lines and convex analysis of 3D point clouds
item.description:
Gap and flush measurement between adjacent body panels is a standard quality checkpoint in automotive assembly, yet automating it reliably remains difficult. Contact gauges are slow and require manual positioning; existing vision-based methods often struggle with specular surfaces, varying lighting, and complex curvatures near the gap edges. This paper proposes a fully geometric solution that operates directly on 3D point clouds acquired by a structured light scanner. The method projects the point cloud onto a series of cross-sectional planes perpendicular to the gap direction, applies projection-line fitting to each face of the gap, and uses convex analysis to robustly locate the gap boundary even when points are noisy or non-uniformly distributed. Gap width and surface flush are then computed analytically from the fitted geometric primitives, without thresholding or image segmentation. Validated on real automotive panel assemblies and published in Measurement Science and Technology (2024), the approach achieves measurement accuracy within 0.05 mm across a range of gap widths and panel materials, meeting automotive production tolerances with a fully non-contact, automatable workflow.

Problem setting

Accurate gap measurement between assembled components—such as body panels in automotive manufacturing—is critical for quality control but challenging to automate with contact-based gauges. This work presents a non-contact method that measures gaps directly from 3D point cloud data captured by structured light or laser scanners. The approach projects points onto cross-sectional planes, fits boundary lines to each gap face, and applies convex analysis to robustly identify the gap edges even in the presence of noise and surface curvature.

item.title: Weighted Point Cloud Normal Estimation
item.description:
Accurate surface normals are essential for nearly every 3D geometry processing pipeline, from Poisson surface reconstruction to ambient occlusion rendering. The standard approach—fitting a plane to each point’s k-nearest neighbours via PCA—is fast but fragile: near sharp edges, neighbours from both sides of the feature contribute equally, averaging out to an erroneous normal; in noisy regions, outlier neighbours corrupt the plane fit. This paper proposes a learned weighted normal estimation scheme that addresses both failure modes. For each query point, a lightweight network predicts a scalar weight for each neighbour based on its geometric relationship to the query—distance, angle deviation from a provisional normal estimate, and local density. The weighted neighbourhood is then used for a robust plane fit that suppresses the contribution of cross-feature and outlier neighbours. The weighting network is small enough to process millions of points per second on a standard GPU. Evaluated on standard normal estimation benchmarks and presented at ICME 2023, the method reduces mean angular error over PCA baselines at edges and noisy regions while remaining competitive with significantly heavier learning-based estimators.

Problem setting

Point cloud normal estimation—computing a unit surface normal at each 3D point—is a foundational pre-processing step for surface reconstruction, rendering, and shape analysis. Standard PCA-based methods treat all neighbours equally, leading to inaccurate normals near sharp features or in the presence of noise and outliers. This paper proposes a weighted normal estimation scheme that assigns adaptive weights to each neighbouring point based on geometric consistency with the local surface model.

item.title: Random screening-based feature aggregation for point cloud denoising
item.description:
Feature aggregation is a core operation in learning-based point cloud denoising: for each noisy point, features from its neighbourhood are pooled to estimate a clean position. The quality of aggregation depends critically on which neighbouring points are included—outlier points and locally dense clusters can dominate the pooled feature and pull the estimate off the true surface. This paper proposes random screening as a lightweight solution: instead of aggregating over the full neighbourhood, multiple random subsets are drawn and screened by a consistency criterion that favours subsets whose geometric statistics match the expected local surface model. Only the highest-scoring subsets contribute to the final aggregated feature. This stochastic screening process is differentiable and integrable into existing denoising architectures as a drop-in replacement for standard neighbourhood aggregation. No additional training data or network redesign is required. Evaluated on ShapeNet3D and real LiDAR scan benchmarks and published in Computers & Graphics (2023), random screening-based aggregation consistently improves Chamfer distance and point-to-mesh accuracy over deterministic aggregation, with the largest gains on point clouds with high outlier rates.

Problem setting

Point cloud denoising methods based on feature aggregation compute noise-free position estimates by aggregating information from local neighbourhoods. Fixed neighbourhood selection is, however, sensitive to outlier points and non-uniform sampling, which can corrupt the aggregated features. This paper introduces random screening-based feature aggregation, where multiple random subsets of each neighbourhood are sampled and screened before aggregation.

item.title: Towards uniform point distribution in feature-preserving point cloud filtering
item.description:
Point cloud filtering must balance two competing objectives: suppressing noise while keeping sharp edges and corners intact. Methods that prioritise feature preservation typically allow point positions to cluster near high-curvature regions, producing non-uniform densities that degrade downstream applications such as surface reconstruction, rendering, and registration. This paper makes the observation that uniformity and feature preservation can be simultaneously achieved by decoupling the two objectives into complementary optimisation terms. A normal-guided feature detection step classifies each point as belonging to a sharp feature, a flat region, or a smooth curve, and assigns an appropriate filtering kernel. A spatial regularisation term then repels neighbouring points that have drifted too close together while attracting those that are too sparse, independently of the feature labels. The joint optimisation converges to filtered point clouds that are both feature-sharp and spatially uniform. Validated on ShapeNet and scanned real-world objects and published in Computational Visual Media (2023), the method outperforms dedicated feature-preserving and uniformity-enforcing baselines in isolation, and is particularly beneficial as a pre-processing step before Poisson surface reconstruction.

Problem setting

Feature-preserving point cloud filtering removes acquisition noise while retaining sharp geometric features such as edges and corners. However, most existing methods do not control the spatial distribution of filtered points, often producing uneven sampling densities: points cluster near sharp features while flat regions become sparse. This paper proposes a filtering approach that jointly optimises for feature preservation and uniform spatial distribution.

item.title: Iteratively weighted principal component analysis and orientation consistency for normal estimation in point cloud
item.description:
Estimating accurate surface normals is a prerequisite for point cloud surface reconstruction, rendering, and geometric analysis. The standard PCA approach fits a plane to each point’s k-nearest neighbours and uses the smallest eigenvector as the normal estimate. This works well on clean, uniformly sampled point clouds but degrades in two common practical situations: in the presence of noise and outliers, which corrupt the covariance matrix, and near sharp features, where neighbours from geometrically different surface patches mix and produce averaged, incorrect normals. This paper addresses both problems. The iteratively re-weighted PCA (IWPCA) assigns lower weights to neighbours that deviate from the current normal estimate and iterates until convergence, effectively ignoring outliers and cross-feature contamination without requiring explicit outlier detection. An orientation consistency propagation step then resolves the normal sign ambiguity inherent to PCA-based estimation: starting from seed points with reliably oriented normals, consistent orientation is propagated across the cloud via a minimum spanning tree, without user interaction. Published in the International Journal of Wireless and Mobile Computing (2020), IWPCA yields more accurate angular errors than standard PCA and achieves globally consistent normal orientation on datasets with sharp features and moderate noise.

Algorithm principle

The method estimates normals by iteratively re-weighting each point’s local neighborhood so that outliers and cross-feature neighbours contribute less to the covariance estimate. A follow-up orientation propagation step resolves the normal sign ambiguity across the point cloud.
